Remaining  Gaps  and  Controversies:  Despite 
remarkable  progress  in  designing  and  preclinically 
validating  hybrid  hydrogels  for  gynecologic  oncol-

nistic  interplay  between  specific  nanomaterials  (e.g., 
graphene  oxide,  PLGA  nanoparticles)  and  the  com-
plex tumor microenvironment remains poorly defined, 
with  conflicting  reports  on  how  hydrogel  stiffness 
and  degradation  by-products  influence  ovarian  ver-
sus cervical cancer cell behaviour. Second, a lack of 
standardized metrics for mesh size, crosslink density, 
and rheological properties hinders direct comparison 
across  platforms  and  laboratories.  Third,  immuno-
genicity  remains  controversial:  although  genipin-
crosslinked  chitosan  matrices  have  been  reported  to 
elicit  minimal  inflammation,  other  studies  document 
macrophage  activation  and  fibrotic  encapsulation 
with similar chemistries. Fourth, the optimal stimuli-
responsive  trigger  (pH,  enzyme,  thermal,  or  light)  is 
still debated, as few head-to-head evaluations exist to 
determine which cue offers the best spatial–temporal 
control in vivo. Finally, the translational gap is strik-
ing—only  a  handful  of  formulations  have  entered 
early‐phase  clinical  trials,  underscoring  challenges 
in  scaling,  sterilization,  regulatory  compliance,  and 
long-term  safety.  Addressing  these  controversies 
through  rigorous  mechanistic  studies,  harmonized 
testing protocols, and coordinated multi-center efforts 
will  be  vital  to  accelerate  the  clinical  translation  of 
hybrid hydrogels in gynecologic cancer care.

Innovations on the horizon

Emerging  technologies  and  materials  offer  potential 
solutions  to  these  challenges.  One  such  innovation 
is  developing  smart  hydrogels  which  can  respond  to 
multiple stimuli, such as pH, temperature, and enzy-
matic activity. They can provide more controlled and 
localized  drug  release,  enhancing  the  precision  of 
cancer  treatments(Yu  et  al.  2022).  Advanced  nano-

agents  within  the  hydrogel  matrix,  creating  complex 
tissue  constructs  that  closely  mimic  natural  tissues. 
This  technology  could  revolutionize  hybrid  hydrogel 
fabrication,  making  them  more  consistent  and  scal-
able for clinical use. By enhancing the precision and 
scalability  of  these  materials,  3D  bioprinting  holds 
the  potential  to  significantly  improve  the  effective-
ness and accessibility of hybrid hydrogels in medical 
applications(Zhou  et  al.  2021).  Innovations  in  gene 
editing  and  molecular  biology  are  enhancing  hybrid 
hydrogels. Techniques like CRISPR-Cas9 can modify 
the genetic makeup of cells within hydrogels, boost-
ing  their  regenerative  capabilities  and  cancer  resist-
ance. Additionally, incorporating engineered extracel-
lular vesicles (EVs) into hydrogels improves targeted 
drug delivery and tissue regeneration. These advance-
ments  could  significantly  improve  the  effectiveness 
of  hybrid  hydrogels  in  medical  applications,  making 
them more adaptable and powerful for various thera-
peutic uses(Ma et al. 2023).

Future research needs

To  fully  realize  the  potential  of  hybrid  hydrogels  in 
gynecological  cancer  treatment,  further  investigation 
is  needed  in  several  areas.  Comprehensive  studies 
on  long-term  biocompatibility  and  biodegradability 
are vital for safety and efficacy. Research should also 
optimize  the  mechanical  characteristics  of  hydrogels 
to  match  different  tissue  requirements,  focusing  on 
the  effects  of  nanomaterials  and  crosslinking  meth-
ods.  Developing  standardized  fabrication  protocols 
will  ensure  consistency  and  reproducibility,  facilitat-
ing  clinical  translation.  Additionally,  clinical  trials 
are  necessary  to  evaluate  efficacy,  side  effects,  and 
patients’ life quality across diverse populations.

Although separate lines of investigation have dem-
onstrated the feasibility of targeted drug delivery and 
tissue  regeneration  in  gynecologic  settings,  evidence 
for  their  concurrent  implementation  within  a  sin-
gle  hydrogel  platform  remains  scarce.  For  instance, 

folate-conjugated 
doxorubicin–loaded 
liposomal 
hydrogels have been shown to enhance drug accumu-
lation and antitumor efficacy in ovarian cancer mod-
els,  whereas  distinct  growth  factor–laden  hydrogel 
scaffolds  have  successfully  supported  endometrial 
repair in rodent studies. To date, few reports describe 
the  co-encapsulation  of  cytotoxic  and  regenerative 
cues within the same construct, and their performance 
in orthotopic gynecologic cancer models has yet to be 
validated.  Bridging  these  trajectories  by  engineering 
dual-payload  hydrogels  could  enable  simultaneous 
eradication of residual malignancy and restoration of 
normal  tissue  architecture,  representing  a  promising 
frontier for multifunctional platform development.

Preclinical models for evaluating hybrid hydrogels

Preclinical  models  that  most  faithfully  recapitulate 
the  gynecologic  tumor  microenvironment  include 
patient-derived  xenografts  (PDXs)  of  high-grade 
serous  ovarian  and  endometrial  cancers  implanted 
orthotopically  into  immunodeficient  mice,  which 
preserve  native  stromal  architecture  and  ECM  com-
position;  syngeneic  models  such  as  ID8  in  C57BL/6 
mice,  providing  an  intact  immune  milieu  and  peri-
toneal  dissemination;  genetically  engineered  mouse 
models (e.g., MISIIR-TAg) that develop spontaneous 
ovarian  neoplasms  with  desmoplastic  stroma  in  an 
immunocompetent  setting;  and  rapid,  cost-effective 
assays like the chicken chorioallantoic membrane and 
zebrafish  xenografts  for  early  screening  of  hydrogel 
biocompatibility,  angiogenic  potential,  and  matrix 
remodeling. By employing this complementary panel, 
researchers  can  robustly  evaluate  in  vivo  gel  rheol-
ogy,  degradation  kinetics,  controlled  release,  and 
downstream  effects  on  vascularization  and  immune 
infiltration,  thereby  streamlining  translational  devel-
opment of hybrid hydrogels in gynecologic oncology.

Advances in hybrid hydrogel design for biomedical 
applications: innovations in drug delivery and tissue 
engineering for gynecological cancers

Hua Chang · Heng Wei · Yue Qi · Silu Ding · 
Hui Li · Si Si

Received: 27 March 2025 / Accepted: 22 June 2025

Abstract  Hybrid  hydrogels  have  emerged  as  mul-
tifunctional  biomaterials  for  targeted  drug  delivery 
and  tissue  engineering  in  gynecologic  oncology.  In 
this  review,  we  summarize  recent  advances  in  the 
design of hybrid hydrogels that combine polymer net-
works with nanomaterials to achieve tunable stimuli-
responsiveness,  enhanced  mechanical  strength,  and 
improved  biocompatibility.  For  example,  preclini-
cal  studies  of  folate‐conjugated  liposomal  doxoru-
bicin have demonstrated enhanced accumulation and 
antitumor  efficacy  in  ovarian  cancer  models,  while 
growth  factor–loaded  hydrogel  scaffolds  have  sup-
ported  endometrial  repair  in  rodent  models.  We

(2) Localized implantation ensures sustained chemo-
therapeutic  concentration  at  residual  tumor  sites,

(3)  Nanoparticle-reinforced  scaffolds  support  pelvic 
tissue  regeneration  post-resection  while  providing 
immunomodulatory cues.

Keywords  Hybrid hydrogels · Drug delivery · 
Tissue engineering · Gynecological cancers

Introduction

Gynecological  cancers  are  malignant  neoplasms  of 
the female reproductive tract, including ovarian, cer-
vical, endometrial (uterine), vulvar, and vaginal can-
cers.  Among  these,  ovarian  and  cervical  cancers  are 
the most prevalent and pose significant health risks to 
women worldwide (Hollis 2023; Nebgen et al. 2019). 
Ovarian  cancer,  often  diagnosed  at  a  late  stage  due 
to  non-specific  symptoms,  remains  the  most  lethal 
gynecological  disease(Karnezis  et  al.  2017).  Cervi-
cal cancer patients usually contracted persistent high-
risk human papillomavirus (HPV), which has seen a 
decline  in  incidence  due  to  screening  programs  and 
HPV vaccination. However, cervical cancer still rep-
resents a major health burden in worldwide low- and 
middle-income  countries  (Burd  2003;  Sharma  et  al. 
2020).

The  treatment  of  gynecological  cancers  typically 
involves a combination of surgery, chemotherapy, and 
radiotherapy  (Ferrall  et  al.  2021;  Koh,  et  al.  2019). 
Despite  advances  in  these  conventional  modalities, 
significant  challenges  remain.  Although  surgical 
resection  effectively  removes  gross  tumor  masses,  it 
often leaves behind microscopic residual disease that 
can lead to recurrence (Kahn et al. 2023; Vergote et al. 
2011).  Chemotherapy,  although  a  cornerstone  in  the 
management of advanced-stage cancers, is associated 
with significant systemic toxicity and the progression 
of drug resistance (Stein et al. 2021; Konstantinopou-
los  et  al.  2015;  Kingnate  et  al.  2021).  Radiotherapy, 
while targeted, can unintentionally provide collateral 
damage  to  adjacent  healthy  tissues,  resulting  in  per-
sistent side effects. Additionally, the heterogeneity of 
tumors and the unique microenvironment of gyneco-
logical  cancers  further  complicate  treatment  strate-
gies,  necessitating  the  progression  of  more  effective 
and less toxic therapeutic options (Herrera et al. 2019; 
Dembo  1992;  Mayadev  et  al.  2022).  Efficient  deliv-
ery to gynecologic tumors leverages both passive and 
active targeting strategies. The enhanced permeability 

and  retention  (EPR)  effect  allows  nanoscale  carri-
ers  to  preferentially  accumulate  in  ovarian  and  uter-
ine  tumors  within  the  peritoneal  cavity  due  to  leaky 
vasculature and impaired lymphatic drainage. Active 
targeting employs ligands—such as folate, RGD pep-
tides,  or  antibodies  against  folate  receptor  α,  HER2, 
or CD44—to promote receptor-mediated endocytosis 
by  cancer  cells.  Physical  guidance  methods,  includ-
ing magnetic field–directed navigation of iron-oxide-
embedded hydrogels and focused ultrasound–induced 
cavitation,  further  enhance  localization  to  pelvic 
lesions.  Stimuli-responsive  triggers  (e.g.,  acidic  pH, 
elevated  MMP  activity,  redox  gradients,  and  hyper-
thermia)  refine  spatial–temporal  drug  release  within 
the  tumor  microenvironment.  These  fundamental 
mechanisms  underpin  the  subsequent  development 
of  hybrid  hydrogel  vectors  tailored  for  gynecologic 
oncology applications.

However, current approaches fail to bridge the gap 
between  these  clinical  limitations  and  precise,  local-
ized  therapy.  For  instance,  residual  microscopic  dis-
ease  after  surgery  can  evade  systemic  chemotherapy, 
and drug-resistant tumor subclones frequently emerge 
when  drug  concentrations  fluctuate  between  sub-
therapeutic  and  toxic  levels.  Hybrid  hydrogels  can  be 
engineered to address each of these issues as follows: 
(1)  Residual  disease  after  surgery:  Hybrid  hydrogels 
can  be  implanted  or  injected  into  the  surgical  bed  to 
form  an  in  situ  depot  that  gradually  releases  chemo-
therapeutics  or  immunomodulators,  thereby  targeting 
microscopic foci that might otherwise remain. (2) Sys-
temic  toxicity  and  drug  resistance:  By  encapsulating 
chemotherapeutic  agents  within  a  polymeric  network, 
hybrid  hydrogels  achieve  sustained,  local  drug  con-
centrations  that  remain  above  the  resistance-threshold 
in tumor cells while sparing healthy tissues from high 
systemic  exposure.  (3)  Collateral  damage  from  radio-
therapy: Hydrogels can be loaded with radioprotective 
nanoparticles  or  antioxidant  compounds  that  release 
selectively in peri-tumoral regions, mitigating damage 
to  adjacent  normal  tissues  during  and  after  radiation. 
(4) Tumor heterogeneity and microenvironmental bar-
riers: Stimuli-responsive hydrogel matrices can exploit 
tumor-specific  cues  (e.g.,  acidic  pH,  elevated  enzyme 
activity) to trigger on-demand drug release, overcom-
ing  barriers  such  as  poor  vascularization  and  hypoxia 
that limit conventional delivery.

At  the  core  of  these  advances  lies  the  integration 
of  nanotechnology  with  well-characterized  polymer

systems.  Specifically,  polyethylene  glycol  (PEG) 
and  chitosan  have  emerged  as  leading  candidates 
for  gynecologic  applications:  PEG-based  hydrogels 
are  renowned  for  their  excellent  biocompatibility, 
“stealth”  properties  (minimized  protein  adsorption), 
and tunable degradation rates. In ovarian cancer mod-
els,  PEG  hydrogels  have  been  formulated  to  release 
cisplatin  over  several  weeks  within  the  peritoneal 
cavity,  maintaining  therapeutic  drug  concentrations 
while reducing nephrotoxicity and myelosuppression. 
Chitosan-based  hydrogels—derived  from  deacety-
lated chitin—offer intrinsic mucoadhesive and hemo-
static  properties  that  are  particularly  advantageous 
for cervical and vaginal delivery. When administered 
intravaginally,  chitosan  matrices  adhere  to  cervical 
mucosa and prolong residence time, improving local 
retention of chemotherapeutics or immunomodulators 
and enhancing uptake by dysplastic epithelial cells.

By  combining 

these  polymers  with 

func-
tional  nanomaterials  (e.g.,  metallic  nanoparticles, 
liposomes,  carbon-based  nanostructures),  hybrid 
hydrogels can be tailored to the mechanical and bio-
logical demands of gynecologic tissues. PEG imparts 
a  hydrophilic,  mesh-like  network  suitable  for  fluid-
rich  peritoneal  environments,  whereas  chitosan  con-
fers  mucoadhesion  and  in  situ  gelation  under  mildly 
acidic vaginal conditions. Such polymer-nanomaterial 
pairings  enable  precise  control  over  swelling  behav-
ior,  degradation  kinetics,  and  drug  release  profiles, 
thereby  addressing  the  specific  clinical  shortcom-
ings  of  surgery,  chemotherapy,  and  radiotherapy  in 
gynecological oncology.

Given the constraints of current therapeutic strate-
gies,  it  is  an  urgency  for  innovative  approaches  that 
can  optimize  therapeutic  outcomes  while  lower  the 
risk of adverse effects. Drug delivery systems specifi-
cally focus on targeting tumor cells, thereby decreas-
ing  systemic  toxicity,  are  of  paramount  importance. 
Similarly, tissue engineering solutions that can facili-
tate  the  regeneration  of  tissues  damaged  by  cancer 
or  its  treatment  are  critical  for  boosting  patient  sur-
vival  and  life  quality  (Fig.  1).  Figure  1  illustrates 
four  complementary  strategies  for  tumor-targeted 
nanotherapy. In panel a, lipid vesicles decorated with 
tumor-specific  antibodies  engage  receptor-mediated 
endocytosis  for  active  targeting;  panel  b  shows  pas-
sive  accumulation  of  nanoparticles  via  the  enhanced 
permeability  and  retention  (EPR)  effect  in  leaky 
tumor  vessels;  panel  c  depicts  magnetic  guidance  of 

chitosan-coated,  5-fluorouracil-loaded  magnetic  nan-
oparticles  under  an  external  magnet  to  concentrate 
the drug at the tumor site; and panel d demonstrates 
focused  ultrasound-induced  cavitation  of  circulat-
ing  microbubbles  to  transiently  disrupt  vascular  bar-
riers  (e.g.,  the  BBB),  thereby  enabling  nanoparticle 
entry—a  mechanism  that  could  be  adapted  to  over-
come  peritoneal  or  pelvic  barriers  in  gynecologic 
cancers. Together, these approaches integrate molec-
ular recognition, physical forces, and barrier modula-
tion  to  enhance  delivery  specificity  and  efficacy,  yet 
each  faces  critical  hurdles—antigen  heterogeneity, 
variable vascular permeability, dosimetry and equip-
ment  logistics  for  external  fields,  and  the  risk  of

delivery and tissue engineering (Ling et al. 2023; Li

and large surface area, can be engineered to function

Hybrid Hydrogels: Composition and Properties

Definition and composition

Hybrid hydrogels are innovative materials that merge 
the  properties  of  traditional  hydrogels  with  those  of 
nanomaterials, creating multifunctional systems ideal 
for advanced biomedical applications (Aliakbarzadeh 
et al. 2024; Ghorbani et al. 2023; Ghahremani-Nasab 
et al. 2025). Hybrid hydrogels are three-dimensional, 
large 
hydrophilic  polymer  networks 

that  retain 

volumes  of  water  while  mimicking  the  extracellular 
matrix  of  native  tissues.  When  these  networks  are 
integrated with nanoscale components—ranging from 
inorganic  nanoparticles  to  polymeric  and  carbon-
based nanostructures—the result is a multifunctional 
platform  that  combines  the  swelling  and  biocompat-
ibility  of  hydrogels  with  the  tailored  properties  of 
nanomaterials  (Pourmadadi  et  al.  2024a,  2024b). 
They are valued for their biocompatibility, flexibility, 
and  ability  to  be  tuned  for  specific  physical  proper-
ties,  rendering  them  appropriate  for  drug  delivery 
and  tissue  engineering  (Wang  et  al.  2021;  Cao  et  al. 
2023).

The  integration  of  nanomaterials  into  hydrogels 
enhances  their  capabilities.  Nanomaterials  including 
nanoparticles,  nanofibers,  and  nanotubes  are  incor-
porated  into  the  hydrogel  matrix  to  impart  unique 
characteristics.  These  include  increased  mechanical 
strength,  responsiveness  to  environmental  changes 
(pH, temperature, or light), and improved drug load-
ing  and  release  profiles  (Qian  et  al.  2022;  Wu  et  al. 
2023; Wang et al. 2024). This combination results in 
a  hybrid  system  where  the  hydrogel  provides  a  bio-
compatible  and  hydrophilic  environment,  while  the 
nanomaterials add functionality, making it possible to 
create  versatile  platforms  for  treating  gynecological 
cancers.  The  increased  mechanical  strength  ensures 
that the hydrogel can withstand physiological stresses 
for  load-bearing  tissues.  Responsiveness  to  environ-
mental  stimuli  permits  the  targeted  release  of  thera-
peutic  agents  upon  encountering  specific  triggers, 
ensuring precise drug delivery towards the tumor site. 
Improved drug loading and release profiles mean that 
higher  doses  of  therapeutic  agents  can  be  incorpo-
rated and transferred in a controlled manner, advanc-
ing the overall efficacy of the treatment. This hybrid 
approach achieves the precise targeting and controlled 
release of drugs, making it a significant advancement 
in  cancer  therapy.  Furthermore,  this  method  mini-
mizes  side  effects  and  maximizes  therapeutic  out-
comes, representing a major step forward in the treat-
ment of gynecological cancers.

These  nanoscale  additives  contribute  to  hybrid 
hydrogel  performance  through  two  complementary 
mechanisms:

Mechanical  reinforcement.  Rigid  nanomaterials 
such  as  carbon  nanotubes  (CNTs),  graphene  oxide 
(GO)  nanosheets  and  silica  nanoparticles  serve  pri-
marily to bolster the hydrogel’s load-bearing capacity

Types of hybrid hydrogels

Interpenetrating networks (IPNs) are a type of hybrid 
hydrogel  comprising  two  or  more  polymer  networks 
that  are  physically  entangled  but  not  covalently 
bonded (Li et al. 2023b). This unique structure allows 
each  polymer  network  to  retain  its  individual  prop-
erties  while  augmenting  the  overall  functionality  of 
the  hydrogel.  The  attributes  of  improving  mechani-
cal strength, swelling capacity, and responsiveness to 
environmental  stimuli  make  them  particularly  fit  for 
drug  delivery  and  tissue  engineering  in  gynecologi-
cal cancer therapy. IPNs provide robust and adaptable 
scaffolds  that  support  cellular  activities  and  transfer 
therapeutic agents effectively (Carpentier et al. 2024). 

In the context of drug delivery, IPNs can accommo-
date  high  drug  loads  and  release  them  in  particular 
physiological  conditions,  concerning  pH  changes 
within  the  TME.  This  release-targeted  mechanism 
guarantees  the  delivering  precision  where  needed, 
lessening  systemic  side  effects  and  boosting  treat-
ment  efficacy.  In  addition,  the  enhanced  mechanical 
strength  and  swelling  capacity  of  IPNs  ensure  that 
they reserve their structural integrity, providing con-
sistent and reliable performance throughout the treat-
ment duration(Wang et al. 2014).

For tissue engineering, IPNs offer a versatile plat-
form  for  creating  scaffolds  that  support  cell  activi-
ties. The physical entanglement of polymer networks 
within  IPNs  provides  a  stable  and  conducive  condi-
tion  for  cellular  activities,  promoting  tissue  regen-
eration  and  restoration  (Chang  and  Yeh  2021).  The 
responsiveness of IPNs to environmental stimuli also 
allows for dynamic modulation of the scaffold’s prop-
erties, adapting to the evolving needs of the regener-
ating  tissue.  This  adaptability  is  helpful  for  treating 
gynecological cancer, due to the need of effective and 
sustained  tissue  regeneration  after  surgical  interven-
tions or radiation therapy (Yang et al. 2021).

Moreover, the ability to incorporate bioactive mol-
ecules and nanomaterials into IPNs further enhances 
their  functionality.  Bioactive  molecules  of  growth 
factors and peptides can be integrated into the hydro-
gel  matrix  to  promote  specific  cellular  responses, 
while nanomaterials can impart additional properties, 
such  as  antimicrobial  activity  or  enhanced  mechani-
cal  strength(Mehmood,  et  al.  2023;  Thankam  et  al. 
2022). This multifunctionality makes IPNs an attrac-
tive  option  for  developing  advanced  therapeutic  and 
regenerative  solutions  tailored  to  the  unique  chal-
lenges of gynecological cancer treatment.

Translating these networks into drug‐delivery depots, 
Sun  et  al.  formulated  an  in  situ  crosslinkable  IPN 
hydrogel  depot  containing  paclitaxel  nanocrystals 
(PNC-gel).  A  single  intraperitoneal  administration 
in  SKOV3-bearing  mice  extended  median  survival 
by 45% compared with Taxol, attributed to sustained 
peritoneal  drug  levels  and  low  systemic  exposure 
(Horst et al. 2022a; Strassburg et al. 2017). Moreover, 
Winer  et  al.  used  F3-targeted  cisplatin-loaded  poly-
acrylamide  IPN  nanoparticles  to  selectively  ablate 
tumor vasculature in both murine and human ovarian 
carcinoma  models,  achieving  rapid  tumor  regression 
and vascular necrosis, even in platinum-resistant lines 
(Horst et al. 2022a; Strassburg et al. 2017).

Core–shell  hydrogels  for  controlled  release,  bio-
degradation  and  imaging.  Core–shell  architectures—
where  a  drug-laden  core  is  enveloped  by  a  degrada-

kinetics, tunable degradation, and integrated imaging 
functions.  An  injectable  DNA–doxorubicin  hydro-

a  72.2%  reduction  in  intraperitoneal  ovarian  tumor 
growth versus free DOX in mice (Horst et al. 2022a; 
Strassburg  et  al.  2017).  Likewise,  thermosensitive 
micelle–hydrogel  hybrids  based  on  Poloxamer  407 
and  carboxymethyl  chitosan  provided  an  initial  20% 
burst  release  of  paclitaxel  followed  by  sustained 
delivery  for  20  days,  achieving  64.3%  tumor  inhibi-

Properties

Firstly,  hybrid  hydrogels  are  characterized  by  bio-
compatibility,  a  fundamental  property  that  allows 
them  to  engage  with  biological  tissues  without  elic-
iting  negative  immune  reactions.  The  hydrophilic 
nature  of  hydrogels,  combined  with  the  inertness  of 
many  nanomaterials,  promotes  cell  behaviors(Zhang 
et  al.  2021;  Sartore,  et  al.  2022).  It  makes  hybrid 
hydrogels  ideal  for  biomedical  fields  for  drug  deliv-
ery  and  tissue  engineering  in  gynecological  cancers. 

The  biocompatibility  of  these  materials  can  be  fur-
ther enhanced by functionalizing them with bioactive 
molecules  or  peptides  that  mimic  the  extracellular 
matrix,  thereby  improving  their  integration  with  the 
surrounding tissue.

Secondly, the mechanical strength of hybrid hydro-
gels  is  vital  for  their  application  in  load-bearing  tis-
sues  and  in  situations  where  structural  integrity  is 
necessary  (Chen  et  al.  2013).  The  incorporation  of 
nanomaterials  containing  carbon  nanotubes,  gra-
phene,  or  silica  nanoparticles  significantly  enhances 
the  mechanical  properties  of  hydrogels.  This  results 
in  materials  that  can  withstand  mechanical  stresses 
and reserve their shape and functionality in dynamic 
physiological environments. In the context of gyneco-
logical cancer treatment, robust hydrogels can provide 
durable  scaffolds  for  tissue  regeneration,  supporting 
the repair and reconstruction of affected tissues.

Thirdly, stimuli-responsive behavior describes how 
hybrid  hydrogels  can  change  physically  or  chemi-
cally when exposed to external stimuli like tempera-
ture,  pH,  light,  or  magnetic  fields  (Wu  et  al.  2010). 
This  property  is  especially  beneficial  for  targeted 
drug  delivery,  enabling  precise  regulation  of  thera-
peutic  agents  triggered  by  external  factors.  pH-sen-
sitive hydrogels can transfer drugs in the acidic con-
dition  of  a  tumor,  ensuring  the  targets  are  delivered 
directly  to  tumor  cells  (Wang,  et  al.  2020)  (Fig.  2).

Design and synthesis of hybrid hydrogels

Chemical Crosslinking

Chemical crosslinking is a critical technique in form-
ing hybrid hydrogels, providing them with necessary 
structural  integrity  and  functionality  for  biomedi-
cal  applications,  especially  in  gynecological  cancer 
treatment.  This  process  contains  constructing  cova-
lent bonds between polymer chains to obtain a stable 
and durable network. Various methods and materials 
are  employed  to  achieve  chemical  crosslinking,  each 
contributing  unique  properties  to  the  final  hydrogel. 
One of the most widely used methods for chemically 
crosslinking  hydrogels  is  free  radical  polymeriza-
tion (Salahuddin et al. 2021). This technique involves 
generating  free  radicals,  which  initiate  the  polym-
erization  of  monomers  to  form  polymer  chains  that 
subsequently  crosslink  (Moncada  et  al.  2023).  Free 
radicals can be generated using thermal initiators, UV 

light, or chemical initiators. This method is versatile, 
permitting  the  addition  of  diverse  functional  groups 
and  nanomaterials  into  the  hydrogel  matrix.  For 
example,  UV-induced  free  radical  polymerization  is 
often employed to create photo-crosslinked hydrogels 
with  precise  control  over  the  network  structure  and 
mechanical properties(Wang et al. 2023).

Additionally,  click  chemistry  represents  a  highly 
specific and efficient approach to chemical crosslink-
ing.  It  involves  reactions  that  form  covalent  bonds 
between  polymer  chains  with  high  yield  and  under 
mild  conditions.  A  prominent  example  is  the  azide-
alkyne cycloaddition, which facilitates the formation 
of  robust  hydrogel  networks(Wang  and  Zhang  2022; 
Singh  et  al.  2022).  The  specificity  and  efficiency  of 
click  chemistry  make  it  particularly  appropriate  for 
biomedical field where precise control over the hydro-
gel’s architecture and functionality is required. Enzy-
matic crosslinking leverages enzymes to catalyze the 
formation of covalent bonds between polymer chains. 
This method is advantageous for its biocompatibility 
and ability to proceed under physiological conditions. 
For instance, horseradish peroxidase (HRP) can cata-
lyze  the  crosslinking  of  phenol-containing  polymers 
within  hydrogen  peroxide(Chen,  et  al.  2025;  Singh, 
et  al.  2025).  Enzymatic  crosslinking  is  particularly 
useful for creating hydrogels intended for tissue engi-
neering  and  regenerative  medicine,  where  maintain-
ing a biological environment is crucial.

Physical crosslinking

Physical  crosslinking  is  a  key  method  for  creating 
hybrid hydrogels, offering benefits like reduced toxic-
ity and the ability to form reversible, stimuli-respon-
sive  networks.  These  interactions  help  form  robust 
yet flexible hydrogels suitable for various biomedical 
applications, particularly where dynamic and respon-
sive properties are needed. Here, we explore various 

physical  crosslinking  techniques  and  their  benefits 
in  biomedical  fields,  especially  in  drug  delivery  and 
tissue  engineering  for  gynecological  cancers.  One 
prevalent  technique  in  physical  crosslinking  is  ionic 
interactions (Sood et al. 2023). This method employs 
multivalent ions to bridge polymer chains, creating a 
gel  network.  It  is  commonly  used  with  natural  poly-
mers like alginate, which gels within divalent cations 
like  calcium  ions  (Ren  et  al.  2024).  The  reversible 
nature  of  ionic  interactions  induces  the  formation  of 
gels  that  respond  to  changes  in  the  ionic  environ-
ment, making them useful for controlled drug release 
applications.

Hydrogen  bonding  is  a  key  method  of  physical 
crosslinking,  formed  between  electronegative  atoms 
and  hydrogen  atoms.  Though  weaker  than  covalent 
bonds,  hydrogen  bonds  offer  enough  stability  for 
applications like drug delivery and tissue scaffolding 
with polymers like PVA and chitosan (Do et al. 2022; 
Lv et al. 2023). Hydrophobic interactions occur when 
nonpolar groups in polymers aggregate in water, often 
used in amphiphilic block copolymers. These interac-
tions  help  form  stable  hydrogel  networks,  useful  for 
encapsulating hydrophobic drugs and releasing them 
in response to environmental changes.

systems, physically crosslinked hydrogels can provide 
a  safe  and  effective  medium  for  controlled  transfor-
mation  of  drug  agents,  reducing  the  risk  of  adverse 
reactions(Yuan et al. 2023). In tissue engineering, the 
capability of physically crosslinked hydrogels to form 
networks through non-covalent interactions including 
hydrogen  bonding,  ionic  interactions,  and  hydropho-
bic  interactions  allows  for  the  creation  of  dynamic 
and  flexible  scaffolds.  These  scaffolds  can  sup-
port  cell  adhesion,  proliferation,  and  differentiation, 
promoting  tissue  regeneration  and  restoration.  The 
reversible  nature  of  physical  crosslinks  also  means 
that  the  hydrogel  can  adapt  to  changes  in  the  physi-
ological  environment,  maintaining  its  functionality 
over time(Reakasame and Boccaccini 2018).

Clinical scalability and regulatory trade-offs: Phys-
ical  crosslinking  techniques—such  as  ionic  gelation, 
thermo- or pH-induced sol–gel transitions, and supra-
molecular host–guest assembly—proceed under mild, 
catalyst-free conditions, preserving labile therapeutics 
and obviating cytotoxic residues. This ease of fabrica-
tion and compatibility with steam or gamma irradia-
tion  sterilization  makes  them  particularly  attractive 
for  point-of-care  vaginal  formulations  (e.g.,  chitosan 
or  alginate  gels  produced  aseptically  at  bedside). 
However,  these  non-covalent  networks  often  exhibit 
lower  mechanical  integrity  and  accelerated  erosion 
under  high-shear  conditions  in  the  peritoneal  cavity 
of  ovarian  cancer  models,  resulting  in  less  predict-
able drug release. By contrast, chemically crosslinked 

PEG  or  genipin-chitosan  hydrogels  deliver  tunable 
crosslink density, enhanced tensile strength, and pro-
longed  in  vivo  residence  suitable  for  both  vaginal 
mucosa  and  intraperitoneal  depots—but  necessitate 
rigorous  removal  of  catalysts  or  photoinitiators  and 
sterile  filtration  steps  to  meet  GMP  and  regulatory 
requirements.

In  summary,  physical  crosslinking  methods  pro-
vide  a  versatile  and  effective  approach  for  develop-
ing  hybrid  hydrogels  with  excellent  biocompatibility 
and  responsiveness.  By  utilizing  non-covalent  inter-
actions  containing  ionic,  hydrogen,  and  hydrophobic 
bonds, these hydrogels offer dynamic, reversible, and 
stimuli-responsive properties that are crucial for drug 
delivery  and  tissue  engineering  applications(Tahir 
et  al.  2025).  The  simplicity  of  the  fabrication  pro-
cess,  combined  with  the  ability  to  customize  hydro-
gel properties, makes physical crosslinking an attrac-
tive  option  for  creating  safe,  efficient,  and  adaptable 
hydrogels for biomedical use, particularly in gyneco-
logical cancer treatment(Miao et al. 2021).

Comparative  Evaluation  of  Crosslinking  Strate-
gies.  Covalent  chemical  crosslinking  methods—
such  as  UV-initiated  free-radical  polymerization  of 
PEG  networks  (Ai  et  al.  2023)  or  strain-promoted 
azide–alkyne cycloaddition (SPAAC) click chemistry 
in PEG–norbornene hydrogels (Jain et al. 2021)—pro-
duce robust covalent bonds that confer high mechani-
cal  strength  (Young’s  modulus  often > 10  kPa)  and 
sustained,  predictable  degradation  profiles  suitable 
for  long-term  peritoneal  drug  depots  (e.g.,  cisplatin 
release  over  several  weeks)  (Shi  et  al.  2023).  How-
ever,  these  approaches  typically  require  potentially 
cytotoxic  photoinitiators  or  catalysts  and  thorough 
post-processing to remove unreacted reagents, which 
can provoke local inflammation. In contrast, physical 
crosslinking—exemplified by  Ca2⁺-mediated gelation 
of  alginate  (Gnanaprakasam  Thankam  and  Muthu 
2014)  or  hydrogen-bonding  in  PVA–chitosan  blends 
(Gong et al. 2023)—occurs under mild, catalyst-free 
conditions,  enabling  injectable,  shear-thinning  gels 
ideal  for  laparoscopic  deployment.  These  non-cova-
lent  networks  avoid  toxic  residues  and  grant  revers-
ible,  stimuli-responsive  behavior,  yet  they  generally 
exhibit  lower  stiffness  (< 1–5  kPa)  and  more  rapid 
erosion under physiological shear, limiting their load-
bearing capacity and release precision. Thus, chemi-
cal  crosslinking  is  preferred  when  structural  resil-
ience  and  tightly  controlled  release  are  paramount,

Self-assembling hydrogels

Self-assembling  hydrogels  are  cutting-edge  biomate-
rials  ideal  for  drug  delivery  and  tissue  engineering, 
especially in gynecological cancers (Fig. 3). The ver-
satile self-assembly mechanisms and broad biomedi-
cal  potential  of  peptide-based  hydrogels  (Fig.  3).  In 
panels  a–c,  short  peptides  exploit  orthogonal  non-
covalent  forces—hydrogen  bonding  to  form  β-sheet 
nanofibers  (a),  ionic  triggers  to  induce  sheet-to-rib-
bon transitions (b), or amphipathic helices that close 
into  ∼16  nm  double-helix  micelles  (c)—to  generate 
three-dimensional  hydrogel  networks.  The  surround-
ing  wheel  highlights  eight  key  application  domains, 
from tissue engineering (a) and targeted intracellular 
drug or gene delivery (b) to neural regeneration (c, d), 
mucosal barrier repair (e), tumor-specific chemother-
apy  (f),  antimicrobial  scaffolds  (g),  and  hemostatic 
dressings  (h).  Such  modular  self-assembly  enables 
precise  control  over  mesh  size,  mechanical  stiff-
ness,  and  stimulus-responsiveness—features  that  can 
be  tuned  to  the  acidic  pH,  protease  activity,  or  ionic 
milieu of the tumor microenvironment, thereby offer-
ing  a  highly  adaptable  platform  for  localized,  con-
trolled  release  and  immunomodulation  in  oncology. 

These hydrogels form spontaneously from individual 
molecules into well-defined structures without exter-
nal  help,  triggered  by  non-covalent  interactions  like 
electrostatic  interactions,  hydrophobic  interactions, 
hydrogen  bonding,  and  van  der  Waals  forces(Zhao 
et al. 2019a). This self-assembly is accompanied with 
unique properties in biomedical fields.

Self-assembling  hydrogels  are  created  by  design-
ing  molecular  building  blocks  that  interact  to  form 
a  3D  network.  These  blocks  include  peptides,  poly-
mers,  and  small  molecules.  Peptide-based  hydrogels 
use  amino  acids  that  develop  structures  of  alpha-
helices or beta-sheets through hydrogen bonding and 
hydrophobic  interactions,  which  then  aggregate  into 
stable  hydrogel  networks(Gnanaprakasam  Thankam 
and  Muthu  2014).  Polymer-based  self-assembling 
hydrogels  often  use  amphiphilic  block  copolymers, 
composed of hydrophilic and hydrophobic segments. 
In  an  aqueous  environment,  the  hydrophobic  seg-
ments  aggregate  to  minimize  water  exposure,  lead-
ing to micelle formation and further organization into 
a  hydrogel.  Additionally,  electrostatic  interactions 
play a role, with charged polymers forming networks 
through attraction or repulsion(Gong et al. 2023).

Self-assembling hydrogels offer significant advan-
tages  in  drug  delivery  because  thsy  can  encapsulate 
and  release  therapeutic  agents  based  on  a  controlled 
mode. Their porous structure allows for incorporating 
diverse drugs, such as small molecules, nucleic acids 
and proteins (Chou and Tsai 2021). The non-covalent

than  50%  of  its  initial  storage  modulus  after  repeated 
peritoneal  contractions  (Zhao  et  al.  2019a;  Ashraful

cyclic compressive strains, retaining over 80% of their

in  vivo  data  confirm  that  self-assembling  systems  can 

withstand the stresses of the pelvic cavity while provid-

Overall,  self-assembling  hydrogels  denotes  a  sig-

innovative solutions for drug delivery and tissue engi-
neering  in  treating  gynecological  cancer.  Their  ability 
to develop functional and versatile structures is a prom-

ing cancer therapy.

Applications in gynecological cancer drug delivery

Targeted drug delivery systems

The  design  of  targeted  drug  delivery  systems  focus 
on  enhancing  the  precision  and  efficacy  of  cancer 
treatment by directing therapeutic agents specifically 
to  tumor  tissues.  The  mechanisms  of  action  in  these 
systems typically contain the use of nanomaterials to 
carry  and  transfer  drugs  within  a  control(Luo  et  al. 
2023).  These  nanomaterials  are  engineered  to  spot 
and  bind  to  specific  molecular  markers  expressed 
on  tumor  cells.  It  guarantees  that  the  drug  payload 
is  concentrated  in  the  tumor  microenvironment.  One 
common  mechanism  refers  to  the  usage  of  ligand-
receptor  interactions.  Ligands,  like  antibodies,  pep-
tides,  or  small  molecules,  are  bind  to  the  surface  of 
nanocarriers(Hennink  and  Nostrum  2002).  These 
ligands specifically interact with overexpressed recep-
tors  on  the  surface  of  cancer  cells.  For  example,  in 
gynecological cancers, overexpressed folate receptors 
are observed on the surface of OV cells. Nanocarriers 
conjugated with folic acid can technically target these 
cells,  facilitating  the  localized  delivery  of  chemo-
therapeutic agents (Dodda et al. 2021; Hu et al. 2022; 
Porfiryeva  et  al.  2024).  Another  mechanism  used  is 
the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect, 
which  takes  advantage  of  the  unique  properties  of 
tumor blood vessels(Cuenot et al. 2022). Tumors have 
leaky  vessels  and  poor  lymphatic  drainage,  allowing 
nanoparticles to accumulate more effectively in tumor 
tissue than in normal tissue. This passive targeting is 
commonly  used  for  nanoparticle-based  drug  deliv-
ery.  Furthermore,  stimuli-responsive  drug  delivery 
systems  release  drugs  in  response  to  specific  tumor 
microenvironment  triggers,  such  as  pH,  tempera-
ture,  or  enzyme  activity.  For  example,  pH-sensitive

Targeted drug delivery systems offer several signif-
icant  advantages  over  traditional  chemotherapy.  The 
primary  benefit  is  the  reduction  in  systemic  toxicity. 
Traditional chemotherapy involves the administration 
of drugs that circulate throughout the body, affecting 
both  cancerous  and  healthy  cells.  This  non-specific 
action  leads  to  serious  side  effects,  including  hair 
loss, nausea, and immunosuppression (Lu and Wang 
2018). In contrast, targeted delivery systems concen-
trate the drugs at the tumor site, thereby reducing col-
lateral harm on normal tissues. Another advantage is 
the improved efficacy of the treatment. By delivering 
more  drugs  directly  to  the  tumor,  these  systems  can 
enhance  the  therapeutic  impact  while  using  lower 
overall  doses  of  the  drug.  It  not  only  maximizes  the 
drug’s  efficacy  but  also  mitigates  the  adverse  effects 
caused by high-dose chemotherapy (Zhu et al. 2024; 
Li et al. 2019).

Gynecologic‐specific  outcomes  and  implications: 
In  the  randomized,  open‐label  phase  III  MIRASOL 
trial (NCT04209855), 453 patients with folate recep-
tor  α–positive,  platinum‐resistant  ovarian  cancer 
received  mirvetuximab  soravtansine  or  investiga-
tor’s‐choice  chemotherapy;  mirvetuximab  signifi-
cantly  extended  median  progression‐free  survival  to 
5.62 months (95% CI, 4.34–5.95) versus 3.98 months 
(95%  CI,  2.86–4.47;  HR  0.65;  P < 0.0001)  and 
median  overall  survival  to  16.46  months  (95% 
CI,  14.46–24.57)  versus  12.75  months  (95%  CI, 
10.91–14.36;  HR  0.67;  P = 0.0046),  while  reducing 
rates  of  grade ≥ 3  adverse  events  (41.7%  vs.  54.1%) 
and discontinuations due to toxicity (9.2% vs. 15.9%) 
(Zhu  et  al.  2024;  Li  et  al.  2019).  Likewise,  a  retro-
spective  cohort  of  69  women  with  recurrent  epithe-
lial  ovarian  carcinoma  treated  with  extended‐dura-
tion  single‐agent  pegylated  liposomal  doxorubicin 
(median  11  cycles,  cumulative  dose  400  mg/m2) 
reported  a  median  PFS  of  13.0  months  (95%  CI, 
10.7–15.2) and median OS of 40.2 months (95% CI, 
30.0–49.0),  with  a  59.4%  clinical‐benefit  rate  (com-
plete  response  17.4%,  partial  response  13.0%,  sta-
ble  disease  29.0%)  and  acceptable  grade ≥ 3  derma-
tologic  toxicity  (31.9%)  (Zhu  et  al.  2024;  Li  et  al. 
2019).  These  gynecologic‐specific  data  demonstrate 
that ligand‐targeted and EPR‐based nanocarriers can 
deliver both survival gains and improved tolerability 
in ovarian cancer. Moving forward, optimizing patient 

selection  via  FRα  expression,  refining  dosing  sched-
ules, and incorporating predictive biomarkers will be 
crucial  to  maximize  therapeutic  index  and  broaden 
application to other gynecologic malignancies.

Additionally,  targeted  drug  delivery  systems  can 
overcome  multidrug  resistance  (MDR)  in  treating 
cancer.  MDR  often  results  from  the  overexpression 
of  efflux  pumps  in  cancer  cells  that  expel  therapeu-
tic  agents,  reducing  their  effectiveness  (Xing  et  al. 
2022a). Nanocarriers can bypass these efflux pumps, 
ensuring that the drug remains inside the cancer cells 
long  enough  to  exert  its  therapeutic  effect.  The  ver-
satility of nanomaterials used in targeted drug deliv-
ery also allows for the combination of diagnostic and 
therapeutic  functions.  These  technologies  support 
simultaneous imaging and therapy of tumors, provid-
ing  instant  feedback  on  the  treatment’s  progress  and 
allowing for adjustments as needed.

Case studies and clinical trials

The  application  of  targeted  drug  delivery  systems 
using hybrid hydrogels and nanomaterials has shown 
promising  results  in  the  treatment  of  gynecological 
cancers.  One  notable  example  is  the  use  of  folate-
conjugated liposomal doxorubicin for ovarian cancer 
treatment (French et al. 2016; Casadidio et al. 2025; 
Zhao  et  al.  2019b).  In  this  approach,  doxorubicin,  a 
potent  chemotherapeutic  agent,  is  encapsulated  in 
liposomes  conjugated  with  folic  acid  (Xing  et  al. 
2022b).  This  allows  the  drug  to  specifically  target 
ovarian  cancer  cells  overexpressing  folate  receptors. 
Clinical  studies  have  demonstrated  that  this  targeted 
delivery  significantly  reduces  the  systemic  toxic-
ity  commonly  associated  with  doxorubicin,  while 
enhancing  its  efficacy  against  ovarian  tumors  (Liu, 
et  al.  2022;  Lima-Sousa  et  al.  2023).  Another  suc-
cessful  application  involves  the  use  of  poly  (lactic-
co-glycolic  acid)  (PLGA)  nanoparticles  loaded  with 
paclitaxel  for  cervical  cancer  (Ak  et  al.  2018;  Zou 
et al. 2012). PLGA nanoparticles provide a sustained 
and  controlled  release  of  paclitaxel,  which  is  crucial 
for  maintaining  therapeutic  drug  levels  at  the  tumor 
site.  Clinical  trials  have  shown  that  patients  receiv-
ing paclitaxel-loaded PLGA nanoparticles experience 
fewer  side  effects  and  improved  tumor  regression 
compared  to  those  receiving  traditional  paclitaxel 
treatment  (Corbin  et  al.  2013;  Hu  et  al.  2025;  Braet 
et al. 2023).

Scaffold design and function

Scaffolds  function  in  tissue  engineering,  particu-
larly  in  the  treatment  of  gynecological  cancers, 
where  tissue  damage  and  loss  often  accompany 
tumor resection and other therapeutic interventions 
(Lawrie,  et  al.  2013a).  The  primary  function  of  a 
scaffold  is  to  provide  a  three-dimensional  structure 
that supports cell attachment, proliferation, and dif-
ferentiation,  promoting  functional  tissue  regenera-
tion.  Scaffolds  are  engineered  to  mimic  the  ECM

The  design  of  scaffolds  needs  to  think  about  sev-

mechanical  strength,  and  biocompatibility.  Poros-

sion,  cell  infiltration,  and  waste  removal  within  the 
scaffold  (Wang  et  al.  2022).  An  optimal  scaffold 
should have interconnected pores of appropriate size 
to  facilitate  these  processes,  ensuring  that  the  cells 
within the scaffold receive adequate nourishment and 
are  able  to  proliferate  effectively.  Biodegradability 
is  another  key  aspect  of  scaffold  design.  The  scaf-

new  tissue  formation,  ensuring  a  gradual  load  trans-
fer  to  the  new  tissue  without  structural  failure.  Bio-
degradable  polymers,  such  as  PGA,  PLA,  and  their 
copolymers,  are  commonly  used  in  scaffold  fabrica-
tion  for  their  predictable  degradation  profiles  and 
biocompatibility(Lawrie, et al. 2013b).

Mechanical  strength 

is  crucial  for  scaffolds 
designed  for  load-bearing  applications,  making  sure 
they  can  tolerate  physiological  forces  without  suc-
cumbing  to  collapse  or  deformation.  This  is  particu-
larly important in gynecological contexts, such as the 
pelvic floor, which is subjected to significant mechan-
ical  stress.  Incorporating  nanomaterials  like  carbon 
nanotubes  or  graphene  can  enhance  the  mechanical 
properties  of  scaffolds,  providing  additional  support 
while  maintaining  necessary  flexibility(Liu,  et  al. 
2021).  Biocompatibility  is  equally  essential,  ensur-
ing  the  scaffold  does  not  trigger  an  adverse  immune 
response  when  implanted(Xu  et  al.  2020a).  Materi-
als used in scaffold construction should be neither be 
toxic  nor  provoke  an  immune  reaction,  and  promote 
cellular  activities.  Natural  polymers  like  collagen, 
gelatin,  and  alginate  are  gradually  employed  due  to 
their  excellent  biocompatibility  and  capability  to 
mimic the natural ECM.

stresses  up  to ~ 15  kPa  and  peak  dynamic  pressures

of ∼80 mmHg during Valsalva maneuvers) (Thulasi-

by  uniaxial  mechanical  testing  of  human  cadaveric

feasibility of achieving the necessary balance of load-
bearing capacity and compliance in a dynamic pelvic 
environment (Thulasidasan et al. 2017).

Regenerative medicine

The usage of hybrid hydrogels in regenerative medicine 
is particularly beneficial for gynecological applications. 
For  instance,  in  patients  undergoing  surgery  for  ovar-
ian  or  cervical  cancer,  there  is  often  a  need  to  repair 
or reconstruct tissues that have been removed or dam-
aged (Hamoudeh et al. 2008). Hybrid hydrogels can be 
designed to degrade at a controlled rate, allowing them 
to  provide  temporary  support  until  the  newly  regener-
ated tissue is strong enough to function independently. 
This  degradability  is  achieved  by  selecting  appropri-
ate  biodegradable  polymers  PLGA  and  tuning  their 
degradation  kinetics  to  match  the  tissue  regeneration 
rate  (Zhou  et  al.  2022;  Ramezani  Farani  et  al.  2022). 
Moreover, hybrid hydrogels can be functionalized with 
bioactive molecules. These bioactive agents are critical 
for  enhancing  the  regenerative  potential  of  the  hydro-
gels by promoting cellular activities. For example, the 
incorporation of VEGF into the hydrogel can stimulate 
angiogenesis, providing the newly forming tissue with 
a  blood  supply  necessary  for  its  survival  and  function 
(Nigam and Bahadur 2017; Hao et al. 2020).

For  clinical  translation,  hybrid  hydrogels  have 
been  engineered  for  minimally  invasive  implanta-
tion  and  predictable  in  vivo  clearance.  They  can  be 
delivered  through  standard  5–12  mm  laparoscopic 
trocars as shear-thinning precursor solutions that rap-
idly gel in situ under physiological or light-triggered 
crosslinking,  without  requiring  specialized  instru-
ments  (Nigam  and  Bahadur  2017;  Hao  et  al.  2020). 
Upon  implantation,  the  hydrogel  network  supports 
host  cell  infiltration  and  neovascularization,  while 
controlled  enzymatic  degradation  aligns  scaffold 
resorption with new tissue formation over 4–6 weeks. 
Importantly,  incorporating  sequential  immunomodu-
latory  cues—such  as  pro-inflammatory  solvents  that 
drive  early  M1  polarization  followed  by  anti-inflam-
matory  moieties  that  induce  M2  polarization—pro-
motes  efficient  clearance  of  hydrogel  remnants  by 
macrophages  and  minimizes  fibrotic  encapsulation 
(Nigam and Bahadur 2017; Hao et al. 2020).

Clinical applications

The  use  of  hybrid  hydrogels  in  treating  gynecologi-
cal cancer has shown great results in clinical settings. 
For  example,  a  PEG-based  hydrogel  loaded  with 
doxorubicin has been tested for ovarian cancer. Clini-
cal  trials  demonstrated  tumor  reduction  with  fewer 
side  effects  than  traditional  chemotherapy(Sabbatini 
et al. 2008). The biocompatibility and controlled drug 
release  properties  of  the  hydrogel  provided  a  sus-
tained therapeutic effect, improving patient outcomes. 
This  highlights  the  potential  of  hybrid  hydrogels  as 
an effective and safer alternative in cancer treatment. 
Another  successful  application  involves  the  use  of 
hyaluronic  acid-based  hydrogels  incorporating  cispl-
atin  for  cervical  cancer  (Kotcherlakota  et  al.  2017). 
Clinical trials have indicated that these hydrogels pro-
vide localized, sustained release of cisplatin, resulting 
in improved tumor regression rates and reduced sys-
temic toxicity. The use of hyaluronic acid, showing its 
natural  biocompatibility  to  interact  with  cancer  cell 
receptors, has been instrumental in the success of this 
treatment approach.

Recent  advancements  have  also  seen  the  integra-
tion  of  immunotherapy  with  hybrid  hydrogels.  For 
example,  a  clinical  study  utilized  chitosan-based 
hydrogels  combined  with  checkpoint  inhibitors  for 
treating  endometrial  cancer  (Wang  et  al.  2020).  The 
hydrogel  matrix  facilitated  the  localized  delivery  of 
immune  modulators,  boosting  the  immune  response 
against  cancer  cells  and  demonstrating  significant 
improvements  in  patient  survival  rates.  Thus,  hybrid 
hydrogels  have  shown  great  potential  in  clinical 
applications  for  treating  gynecological  cancer,  giv-
ing  more  effective,  localized,  and  safer  alternatives 

to  conventional  therapies.  Their  ability  to  provide 
controlled drug release, reduce systemic toxicity, and 
enhance immune responses underscores their promis-
ing role in improving patient outcomes and advancing 
cancer care.

Translational  Challenges  and  Clinical  Consid-
erations:  Bringing  hybrid  hydrogels  from  bench  to 
bedside  entails  navigating  complex  regulatory  path-
ways  for  combination  drug–device  products,  often 
requiring  both  an  Investigational  New  Drug  (IND) 
application  and  an  Investigational  Device  Exemp-
tion (IDE), as well as compliance with pharmaceuti-
cal  (e.g.,  21  CFR  210/211)  and  medical-device  (21 
CFR  820)  GMP  standards.  Achieving  batch  con-
sistency  and  scalability  demands  tight  control  over 
polymer  molecular-weight  distributions,  nanoma-
terial  dispersion,  and  crosslink  density—necessi-
tating  validated  in-process  analytics  and  stringent 
quality  acceptance  criteria  for  each  production  run. 
Rigorous  safety  assessment  protocols,  aligned  with 
ISO  10993  biocompatibility  testing  and  GLP  toxi-
cology studies, must evaluate both acute and chronic 
responses, including local inflammation, degradation 
by-products,  and  systemic  exposure  associated  with 
long-term  implantation.  Encouragingly,  early-phase 
clinical  trials  are  now  underway:  phase  I/II  studies 
of  thermosensitive  poloxamer  hydrogels  delivering 
paclitaxel in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer, and of 
hyaluronic acid–cisplatin depots in recurrent cervical 
carcinoma, have reported acceptable local tolerability 
and sustained intratumoral retention, though final effi-
cacy  data  are  pending.  Addressing  these  regulatory, 
manufacturing, and safety hurdles will be essential to 
realize  the  full  clinical  potential  of  hybrid  hydrogels 
in gynecologic oncology.

biocompatibility  and  immune  response.  While  these 
materials  are  designed  to  be  biocompatible,  individ-
ual variations in patient responses can lead to unpre-
dictable  outcomes.  For  instance,  some  patients  may 
experience  inflammatory  reactions  or  fibrosis  at  the 
site of hydrogel implantation, which can compromise

Despite  notable  advances,  several  critical  chal-
lenges hinder the reliable translation of hybrid hydro-
gels for gynecologic applications. First, reproducibil-
ity in hydrogel synthesis remains problematic: minor 
variations in polymer molecular weight, crosslinking 
kinetics, or mixing conditions can yield markedly dif-
ferent  network  architectures  and  mechanical  proper-
ties.  Second,  batch-to-batch  variability—driven  by 
inconsistencies  in  raw-material  purity,  crosslinker 
concentration,  and  processing  parameters—often 
leads  to  unpredictable  drug-loading  efficiencies  and 
degradation  profiles.  Third,  sterilization  protocols 
pose  a  dilemma:  common  methods  such  as  gamma 
irradiation,  autoclaving,  or  ethylene-oxide  treatment 
can  induce  polymer  chain  scission  or  alter  crosslink 
density,  compromising  scaffold  integrity  and  thera-
peutic  payload  stability.  Finally,  in  vivo  degradation 
frequently diverges from in vitro expectations due to 
heterogeneous  enzyme  activity,  localized  pH  shifts, 
and  variable  immune  cell  infiltration  within  the  pel-
vic cavity, resulting in inconsistent scaffold resorption 

and  drug-release  kinetics.  Rigorous  process  control, 
standardized  quality  metrics,  validated  sterilization 
methods, and more predictive animal models will be 
essential  to  overcoming  these  hurdles  and  ensuring 
reproducible clinical performance.

Remaining  Gaps  and  Controversies:  Despite 
remarkable  progress  in  designing  and  preclinically 
validating  hybrid  hydrogels  for  gynecologic  oncol-
ogy,  key  gaps  and  debates  persist.  First,  the  mecha-
nistic  interplay  between  specific  nanomaterials  (e.g., 
graphene  oxide,  PLGA  nanoparticles)  and  the  com-
plex tumor microenvironment remains poorly defined, 
with  conflicting  reports  on  how  hydrogel  stiffness 
and  degradation  by-products  influence  ovarian  ver-
sus cervical cancer cell behaviour. Second, a lack of 
standardized metrics for mesh size, crosslink density, 
and rheological properties hinders direct comparison 
across  platforms  and  laboratories.  Third,  immuno-
genicity  remains  controversial:  although  genipin-
crosslinked  chitosan  matrices  have  been  reported  to 
elicit  minimal  inflammation,  other  studies  document 
macrophage  activation  and  fibrotic  encapsulation 
with similar chemistries. Fourth, the optimal stimuli-
responsive  trigger  (pH,  enzyme,  thermal,  or  light)  is 
still debated, as few head-to-head evaluations exist to 
determine which cue offers the best spatial–temporal 
control in vivo. Finally, the translational gap is strik-
ing—only  a  handful  of  formulations  have  entered 
early‐phase  clinical  trials,  underscoring  challenges 
in  scaling,  sterilization,  regulatory  compliance,  and 
long-term  safety.  Addressing  these  controversies 
through  rigorous  mechanistic  studies,  harmonized 
testing protocols, and coordinated multi-center efforts 
will  be  vital  to  accelerate  the  clinical  translation  of 
hybrid hydrogels in gynecologic cancer care.

Future research needs

To  fully  realize  the  potential  of  hybrid  hydrogels  in 
gynecological  cancer  treatment,  further  investigation 
is  needed  in  several  areas.  Comprehensive  studies 
on  long-term  biocompatibility  and  biodegradability 
are vital for safety and efficacy. Research should also 
optimize  the  mechanical  characteristics  of  hydrogels 
to  match  different  tissue  requirements,  focusing  on 
the  effects  of  nanomaterials  and  crosslinking  meth-
ods.  Developing  standardized  fabrication  protocols 
will  ensure  consistency  and  reproducibility,  facilitat-
ing  clinical  translation.  Additionally,  clinical  trials 
are  necessary  to  evaluate  efficacy,  side  effects,  and 
patients’ life quality across diverse populations.

Although separate lines of investigation have dem-
onstrated the feasibility of targeted drug delivery and 
tissue  regeneration  in  gynecologic  settings,  evidence 
for  their  concurrent  implementation  within  a  sin-

repair in rodent studies. To date, few reports describe 
the  co-encapsulation  of  cytotoxic  and  regenerative 
cues within the same construct, and their performance 
in orthotopic gynecologic cancer models has yet to be 
validated.  Bridging  these  trajectories  by  engineering 
dual-payload  hydrogels  could  enable  simultaneous 
eradication of residual malignancy and restoration of 
normal  tissue  architecture,  representing  a  promising 
frontier for multifunctional platform development.

Preclinical models for evaluating hybrid hydrogels

Preclinical  models  that  most  faithfully  recapitulate 
the  gynecologic  tumor  microenvironment  include 
patient-derived  xenografts  (PDXs)  of  high-grade 
serous  ovarian  and  endometrial  cancers  implanted 
orthotopically  into  immunodeficient  mice,  which 
preserve  native  stromal  architecture  and  ECM  com-
position;  syngeneic  models  such  as  ID8  in  C57BL/6 
mice,  providing  an  intact  immune  milieu  and  peri-
toneal  dissemination;  genetically  engineered  mouse 
models (e.g., MISIIR-TAg) that develop spontaneous 
ovarian  neoplasms  with  desmoplastic  stroma  in  an 
immunocompetent  setting;  and  rapid,  cost-effective 
assays like the chicken chorioallantoic membrane and 
zebrafish  xenografts  for  early  screening  of  hydrogel 
biocompatibility,  angiogenic  potential,  and  matrix 
remodeling. By employing this complementary panel, 
researchers  can  robustly  evaluate  in  vivo  gel  rheol-
ogy,  degradation  kinetics,  controlled  release,  and 
downstream  effects  on  vascularization  and  immune 
infiltration,  thereby  streamlining  translational  devel-
opment of hybrid hydrogels in gynecologic oncology.

Conclusion

Hybrid  hydrogels  show  a  groundbreaking  advance-
ment  in  the  field  of  biomedical  materials,  particu-
larly  for  the  treatment  of  gynecological  cancers. 
These materials combine the beneficial properties of 
hydrogels,  including  high  water  content,  biocompat-
ibility, and flexibility—with the enhanced mechanical

ment  of  hybrid  hydrogels  involves  various  methods 
of chemical and physical crosslinking, each contribut-

crosslinking provides stability and durability through 
covalent  bonding,  while  physical  crosslinking  offers 
reversible  and  stimuli-responsive  properties  through 
non-covalent  interactions.  These  crosslinking  tech-

In  targeted  drug  delivery  systems,  hybrid  hydro-
gels  enable  the  precise  localization  and  controlled 
release  of  therapeutic  agents,  minimizing  systemic 
toxicity and enhancing treatment efficacy. Case stud-
ies  and  clinical  trials  have  demonstrated  the  effec-
tiveness  of  these  systems  in  improving  patient  out-
comes  in  gynecological  cancer  treatment.  Moreover, 
hybrid  hydrogels  contribute  to  tissue  engineering  by 
offering  scaffolds  that  promote  cell  adhesion,  prolif-
eration,  and  differentiation,  thereby  improving  tissue 
regeneration  and  restoration.  Despite  these  advance-
ments, challenges remain in the production, biocom-
patibility, and long-term stability of hybrid hydrogels. 
Addressing  these  issues  through  ongoing  research 
and innovation is essential for optimizing their clini-
cal application.

Hybrid  hydrogels  have  a  significant  potential 
impact on gynecological cancer treatment. They offer 
a  targeted,  less  toxic  alternative  to  traditional  thera-
pies,  delivering  drugs  directly  to  tumors  and  reduc-
ing  side  effects,  which  is  especially  beneficial  for 
chemotherapy  patients.  In  tissue  engineering,  hybrid 
hydrogels  enhance  reconstructive  surgery  outcomes, 
providing better functional and aesthetic results. The 
future of these materials will be driven by innovations 
like  3D  bioprinting  and  smart  hydrogels.  3D  bio-
printing  allows  precise  customization  for  individual 
patients, while smart hydrogels offer on-demand drug 
release, improving cancer therapy’s effectiveness.

In conclusion, hybrid hydrogels represent a versa-
tile and promising platform for targeted drug delivery 
and  tissue  engineering  in  gynecologic  oncology.  By 
combining  polymer  networks  with  functional  nano-
materials,  these  systems  can  achieve  controlled  deg-
radation,  stimuli-responsive  release,  and  mechanical 
properties  tailored  to  pelvic  tissues.  Preclinical  evi-
dence  supports  their  ability  to  localize  therapeutics 
and  guide  regenerative  processes  with  reduced  sys-
temic  toxicity.  Nonetheless,  significant  translational 
gaps  remain.  Standardized,  scalable  manufacturing 
under  Good  Manufacturing  Practice  conditions  must 
be  established  to  ensure  batch‐to‐batch  consistency 
and  regulatory  compliance.  Moreover,  robust  clini-
cal  data  from  well-powered,  randomized  phase  II/
III trials are required to validate safety, immunocom-
patibility, and efficacy across diverse patient popula-
tions. Interdisciplinary collaboration among materials 
scientists,  clinicians,  and  regulatory  bodies  will  be 
essential  to  address  these  challenges.  With  rigorous 
process  control  and  comprehensive  clinical  evalua-
tion, hybrid hydrogels have the potential to augment 
current treatment paradigms in gynecological cancer
